articles.title: In 1999, Metallica singer James Hetfield bought California’s 1,150-acre Luiz Ranch; 19 years later, 1,000 acres entered a Marin Agricultural Land Trust easement
articles.summary: Discover how Metallica's James Hetfield transformed his California ranch into a conserved agricultural landscape, preserving 1,000 acres for future generations.
articles.body: A ranch in Marin County, once owned by a well-known rock musician, later became part of a long-term effort to keep the land in agricultural use. Its owners worked with a local land trust to place much of the ranch under permanent conservation protection. According to the Marin Agricultural Land Trust (MALT), James Hetfield and his wife, Francesca, bought the 1,150-acre Luiz Ranch in 1999, and by 2018 about 1,000 acres had been protected through agricultural conservation easements. The easements prevent development while allowing the Hetfields to retain ownership, with MALT holding and monitoring the restrictions in perpetuity.A ranch built around agricultureLuiz Ranch had a history of being agricultural land before it gained notoriety as a place linked to a renowned singer. As per MALT, the land had a previous history of use as a dairy farm, and the conservation easement sought to restore farming activities on the piece of land by ensuring that it remains in active agricultural use.The protection was assembled over several years rather than in a single transaction. According to KQED, 440 acres were placed under an agricultural conservation easement in 2005, followed by another 320 acres in 2009. In late 2017, the Hetfields offered a further 240 acres. The Marin County Open Space District subsequently consolidated the three easements and transferred them to MALT in 2018. It lists the protected area as 1,008 acres and describes the deal as roughly 1,000 acres intended for ranching.The conserved area was not only an addition but also served as a connecting point between more than 12,000 acres that were being conserved both by MALT and the Open Space District. The deal added a large area of conserved agricultural land in the region. It also included financial assistance in the form of a $175,000 endowment made by the county and the Hetfields to help MALT in its stewardship responsibilities. Instead of being developed, the land remained in agricultural use.Why protecting the landscape mattersThe Luiz Ranch contract is one example of how conservation easements can protect California’s working ranches without taking the land out of private hands. Unlike a public land purchase, a conservation easement allows the owner to keep the property while placing permanent limits on development. Research published in PLOS ONE found that conservation easements can provide long-term protection for California’s rangelands, while still allowing them to remain in agricultural use. The study also noted that these landscapes provide important wildlife habitat and help maintain connections between larger areas of habitat. At Luiz Ranch, that meant the land could continue to be used for cattle grazing rather than being left unused.From celebrity ranch to working landscapeThe conservation history of the ranch also developed alongside debates over development in Lucas Valley. Residents opposed development plans for the property, and a later proposal reduced the housing while increasing the amount of land conserved under the agricultural easement. The end result was that a small portion of the original land remained outside the conservation easement, which was itself expanded to cover 1,000 acres.MALT referred to this contract as protection of a scenic corridor, benefiting the agricultural economy of Marin County and preserving 2.7 miles of stream. The ranch was part of a vast network of conserved agricultural land in Marin County. It remained privately owned even as it was placed under conservation protection. What began as a 1,150-acre property purchase eventually evolved into a conservation agreement. In 2018, approximately 1,000 acres were protected through an agricultural agreement rather than development.See More: In 2017, Jennifer Garner invested in an organic brand and joined it as a co-founder; years later, her stake rose to USD 64 millionThis agreement meant the ranch could continue to function as a working piece of land. Cattle grazing and other agricultural activities could carry on, while the easement placed limits on future development. In this way, the property remained useful to the people working on it while also helping preserve the open, rural character of the surrounding landscape.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Presidente do Água Santa se entrega à polícia após 2 dias foragido; ele é investigado em operação contra o PCC | G1
articles.standfirst: Paulo Sirqueira Korek Farias, o 'Paulo Camarão', é apontado pelo MP e pela Polícia Civil como empresário do setor de transportes e 'testa de ferro' da organização criminosa.
articles.summary: Paulo Sirqueira Korek Farias, o 'Paulo Camarão', é apontado pelo MP e pela Polícia Civil como empresário do setor de transportes e 'testa de ferro' da organização criminosa.
articles.body:
Paulo Korek, conhecido como Paulo Camarão, presidente do Esporte Clube Água Santa, se entregou à polícia em uma delegacia em Mogi das Cruzes, na Grande São Paulo, na noite deste sábado (19). Ele era considerado foragido desde quinta (17).

Korek um dos alvos dos mandados de prisões na Operação Vectura Corrupta, deflagrada pelo Ministério Público (MP) e pela Polícia Civil na quinta (17). A investigação apura a infiltração do Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) no sistema de transporte coletivo da capital.

Segundo a investigação, Paulo Camarão é empresário do setor de transportes, gestor das empresas Translíder e A2 Transportes e apontado como suposto "testa de ferro" da organização criminosa.

O nome de Paulo Sirqueira Korek Farias consta como presidente do Água Santa no cadastro da Federação Paulista de Futebol (FPF). O clube é da cidade de Diadema, na Grande São Paulo. Ele foi fundado em 1981 e profissionalizado em 2011.

'Paulo Camarão', um dos alvos da operação do MP, é presidente do Água Santa, time de futebol vice-campeão paulista de 2023. — Foto: Reprodução/Arquivo pessoal

Sob a gestão de Paulo Camarão, o Água Santa viveu em 2023 o momento de maior destaque de sua história no futebol profissional.

O clube chegou à final do Campeonato Paulista da Primeira Divisão, a elite do futebol estadual, e terminou como vice-campeão . A equipe de Diadema venceu o Palmeiras por 2 a 1 no jogo de ida da decisão, mas perdeu por 4 a 0 na partida de volta. O Palmeiras ficou com o título.

A campanha foi histórica para o Água Santa, que eliminou São Paulo e Red Bull Bragantino antes de chegar à final.

Em 2015, o Água Santa chegou pela primeira vez à elite do Campeonato Paulista. Atualmente, o Água Santa está na Série A2 do Campeonato Paulista, a Segunda Divisão do futebol estadual, depois de ter sido rebaixado em 2025.

Operação investiga infiltração no transporte

Paulo Farias, o 'Paulo Camarão', é presidente do Água Santa, segundo site da Federação Paulista de Futebol. — Foto: Reprodução/FPF

A operação desta quinta-feira investiga a atuação do PCC no setor de transporte coletivo de São Paulo. Segundo o Ministério Público, foram identificadas pelo menos 12 empresas de transporte de passageiros que seriam controladas direta ou indiretamente pela facção.

Entre os alvos está o ex-presidente da Câmara Municipal de São Paulo Milton Leite, que teve a prisão temporária autorizada pela Justiça. Ao todo, a operação cumpre 16 mandados de prisão e 18 de busca e apreensão.

A investigação apura suspeitas relacionadas à atuação do crime organizado no sistema de transporte e à possível participação de pessoas ligadas ao setor empresarial e à política.

articles.title: Marcos Sacramento 'bebe da chama' do samba em show que transpõe a roda do cantor para o palco com certa vibração | G1
articles.body:
Marcos Sacramento na estreia do show 'Sambear' no Circo Voador, no Rio de Janeiro (RJ), na noite de sexta-feira, 18 de setembro — Foto: Michelle Castilho / Divulgação Circo Voador

♬ Em essência, “Sambear” – show estreado por Marcos Sacramento na noite de ontem, sexta-feira, 18 de setembro, no Circo Voador, no Rio de Janeiro (RJ) – é a transposição para o palco da roda “Samba do Sacramento”, comandada pelo cantor fluminense em espaços do centro da cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ).

Por mais que o roteiro encampe uma ou outra música rara na roda, como “Jesus é preto” (Marcos Sacramento e Paulo Baiano), samba autoral composto nos anos 1980 e gravado décadas depois pelo cantor no luminoso álbum “Arco” (2024), o show “Sambear” preserva o espírito de união e congraçamento da roda, além do repertório que celebra o samba nas várias formas do gênero.

Aberto com o tradicional ponto de umbanda “O sino da igrejinha” no canto da big banda, o show tem alta carga de afro-brasilidade e espiritualidade, traduzida nas imagens e símbolos alocados no palco, ao lado do artista. Acima de qualquer credo, “Sambear” representa o manifesto da fé de Marcos Sacramento no samba e no povo da raça Brasil.

Tão musical quanto política, tal manifestação ficou evidente no roteiro desde a primeira música entoada pelo artista no show, “Canto das três raças” (Mauro Duarte e Paulo César Pinheiro, 1976) – samba que ecoou há 50 anos na voz da cantora Clara Nunes (1942 – 1983) – até a última antes do bis, “A batucada dos nossos tantãs” (Sereno, Adilson Gavião e Robson Guimarães, 1993), samba com o qual o grupo Fundo de Quintal fez declaração de resistência de um povo que não perde o prazer de cantar, mesmo quanto tentam silenciá-lo.

Marcos Sacramento celebra a resistência do samba em show derivado da roda do artista — Foto: Michelle Castilho / Circo Voador

Sim, foi bonito de se ver Sacramento correndo pelo palco do Circo Voador, dando voz a um punhado de sambas cantados pelo artista sob a batuta de uma banda com o peso de uma orquestra.

Essa banda incluía virtuoses como o violonista Luiz Flavio Alcofra, o multi-instrumentista Elísio Freitas – cujo solo de guitarra sublinhou o sentimento posto pelo artista “Você me vira a cabeça (Me tira do sério)” (Chico Roque e Paulo Sérgio Valle, 2001), número teatral já recorrente na roda de Sacramento – e o cavaquinhista Lucas Machado, que conquistou a plateia com os improvisos de partideiro feitos no samba “Alguém me avisou” (Dona Ivone Lara, 1980).

Poucas vezes o Circo Voador esteve tão vazio (até pela concorrência de shows gratuitos realizados na mesma noite no bairro da Lapa) como na estreia de “Sambear”, mas Sacramento não se intimidou e apresentou show quente. O calor vinha tanto do canto do solista quanto dos caprichados arranjos tocados pela banda que abarcava cordas, sopros e percussões.

A seleção de repertório, às vezes óbvia, contribuiu para facilitar a absorção do show por uma plateia animada, mas não exatamente vibrante. Em números como “Sem compromisso” (Geraldo Pereira e Nelson Trigueiro, 1944) e “Samba do grande amor” (Chico Buarque, 1983), pareceu que a vibração era maior no palco do que na pista do Circo Voador.

Ainda assim, ninguém ficou imune à exuberância e à teatralidade do canto de “Disseram que eu voltei americanizada”(Luiz Peixoto e Vicente Paiva, 1940), samba recorrente na roda de Sacramento e no qual o intérprete destila finas ironias e mostra impressionante senso rítmico.

Entre exaltações aos pioneiros bambas do bairro carioca do Estácio – reverenciados com as lembranças dos sambas “Se você jurar” (Ismael Silva e Nilton Bastos, 1931) e “Nem é bom falar” (Ismael Silva, Nilton Bastos e Francisco Alves, 1931) – e à cantora Clementina de Jesus (1901 – 1987), saudada com “Yaô” (Pixinguinha e Gastão Vianna, 1938) e “Benguelê” (Pixinguinha e Gastão Viana, 1946), Marcos Sacramento puxa no roteiro de “Sambear” uma linha que vai até as contemporâneas Manu da Cuíca e Marina Iris, parceiras no samba “Virada” (2021).

Esse fio imaginário passou por Ivone Lara (1922 – 2018) e pela ideologia de Jorge Aragão, presente no roteiro com “Identidade” (Jorge Aragão, 1992), manifesto de orgulho negro.

Enfim, ao sair do palco do Circo Voador após o bis, no qual cantou “Vou festejar” (Jorge Aragão, Dida e Neoci Dias, 1978), Marcos Sacramento deixou boa impressão, mas também a sensação de que o show “Sambear” precisa se desprender mais da roda “Samba do Sacramento” para ganhar vida própria.

Marcos Sacramento estreia o show 'Sambear' com alta carga de espiritualidade afro-brasileira — Foto: Michelle Castilho / Divulgação Circo Voador

articles.title: Pato Fu lança em outubro álbum ao vivo em que rebobina o disco 'Gol de quem?' com BNegão, Tom Zé e Zélia Duncan | G1
articles.body:
O grupo Pato Fu perpetua em álbum o show de 2025 em que celebrou os 30 anos do segundo álbum da banda, 'Gol de quem?', lançado em 1995 — Foto: Fabiana Figueiredo / Divulgação

♬ Em 7 de agosto de 2025, o grupo Pato Fu subiu ao palco do Audio Club, reduto roqueiro da cidade de São Paulo (SP), para apresentar show comemorativo dos 30 anos do segundo álbum de estúdio da banda mineira, “Gol de quem?”, disco produzido pelo engenheiro de som Carlos Savalla e lançado em 1995 pelo selo Plug da gravadora BMG.

O show foi gravado e, um ano depois, gera o álbum “Gol de quem? – Ao vivo”, programado para ser lançado em 9 e outubro em edição digital e posteriormente em CD e LP duplo, em data ainda incerta.

BNegão , Coral, Tom Zé e Zélia Duncan participaram do show em intervenções perpetuadas no álbum “Gol de quem? – Ao vivo”. O registro audiovisual do show será exibido em 10 de outubro pelo canal Music Box Brazil.

Bem recebido pela crítica, que detectava ecos do grupo Os Mutantes no som alternativo da banda que surgira em 1992 em Belo Horizonte (MG), o álbum “Gol de quem?” ampliou o público do Pato Fu com músicas como “Sobre o tempo” (John Ulhoa, 1995), face mais pop de repertório que incluía recriações de “A volta do boêmio” (Adelino Moreira, 1957) – um dos maiores sucessos do cantor Nelson Gonçalves (1919 – 2018) – e “Qualquer bobagem” (Arnaldo Baptista, Rita Lee, Sérgio Dias e Tom Zé, 1969), música lançada no segundo álbum de estúdio do grupo Os Mutantes.

Sem falar na lembrança de “Vida de operário” (Falcão), música apresentada pela banda punk Excomungados nos anos 1980, gravada pela Patife Band em 1987 e registrada pelo grupo paulistano em disco no EP “Pela primeira vez no paraíso” (1990).

Todas essas músicas são rebobinadas por Fernanda Takai (voz), John Ulhoa (guitarra), Ricardo Koctus (baixo), Richard Neves (teclados) e Xande Tamietti (bateria e percussão) no álbum “Gol de quem? – Ao vivo” sob direção musical de Ulhoa.

“Sobre o tempo” reaparece em feat do Pato Fu com Zélia Duncan. “A volta do boêmio” retorna com a adesão de BNegão. “Qualquer bobagem” ganha a voz de Tom Zé, um dos compositores da música gravada pelo artista em álbum de 1970, um ano após o registro original dos Mutantes. Já Coral entra em cena em “Sertões” (Ricardo Koctus, 1995), uma das músicas autorais apresentadas pelo Pato Fu no álbum “Gol de quem?”.

Capa do álbum 'Gol de quem? – Ao vivo', do grupo Pato Fu — Foto: Divulgação

articles.title: In 1997, Paul Newman donated 7.5 acres of his land to Westport; 14 years later, his dream of turning it into a preserve came true in the form of a 39-acre protected land
articles.summary: Discover how Paul Newman transitioned from Hollywood star to environmental advocate by donating land for conservation. Learn about the Newman-Poses Nature Preserve and its significance in Westport, Connecticut.
articles.body: Over the years, many celebrities have invested their time and funds to support the causes they believe in. Did you know that actor Paul Newman, who is best known for projects like ‘The Color of Money,' ‘The Hustler,' ‘Cat on a Hot Tin Roof,' ‘Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid,' and many others, once ended up donating a large part of his property for conservation benefits in 1997? Here is what you need to know about how and why the actor made this move.In 1997, Paul Newman donated 7.5 acres to Connecticut’s WestportIn his hometown, the Oscar-winning actor and his wife, actress Joanne Woodward, donated around 7.5 acres of land that was adjacent to their home to the Town of Westport. The celebrity duo made the move to prevent real estate development in the area, according to reports shared online by The Connecticut Post.Later in 1997, the town of Westport purchased around 30 acres of surrounding land for USD 3.75 million. They bought the land from Lillian Pose’s family, who were close to the Newmans and their neighbors. She also served as the former attorney in FDR's presidential administration. Woodward also donated around 8 acres of his land to the town. Years later, the donated land combined to create the Newman-Poses Nature Preserve.14 years after he made the sale, Paul Newman’s donated land turned into a nature preserveThe idea to turn the land into a nature preserve came from the Oscar-winning actor; however, he sadly passed away in 2008, before the preserve could be officially established. In a report published by the Aspetuck Land Trust, the company that works on protecting open space in Westport, Weston, Fairfield, and Easton, it was revealed that Newman was highly supportive of the efforts to turn the large land area into a preserve.At the time, Jonathan Wagner, who was the chairman of the land acquisition committee, shared details on how Newman highly supported the organization's conservation work. The actor also provided financial support for the cause, which included the acquisition of Trout Brook Valley in Weston.The Newman Poses Nature Preserve officially opened to the public on May 1, 2011, almost three years after the star passed away after fighting a battle with lung cancer. The 38-acres now sit around Bayberry Lane, Coleytown Road, and Easton Road in Westport. The preserve also includes woods, a meadow, wetlands, and the Aspetuck River.After his passing, his daughters actively carried out his dream and worked with the organization that set the preserve up and now manages it as well. The name, which was meant to honor both Newman and Poses, was approved in 2010 during a Westport Representative Town Meeting.While most of the land is protected now, the company that manages the land has set up a separate recreational area for activities where people can walk around, spend some time, and even fish in some locations.The preserve has now become part of Newman’s legacy as an actor and an activist who stood by what he believed in most.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.title: Kristen Bell Reveals She Planned Her “Frozen” Sing-Along with Savannah Bananas Herself (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Bell tells PEOPLE the performance was “a freaking dream come true”
articles.body:
Kristen Bell tells PEOPLE that she planned her Frozen sing-along with the Savannah Bananas herself

"That was an incoming call for them," she says

The actress sang "For the First Time in Forever" as part of a medley at the baseball team's game in Denver on Aug. 15

Kristen Bell was the one pitching when it came to her team-up with the Savannah Bananas baseball team.

The actress, 46, made a surprise appearance at the Bananas' Aug. 15 game in Denver to perform a musical medley with Broadway star Derek Klena that included a Frozen favorite. While chatting exclusively with PEOPLE as part of her partnership with Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days , Bell revealed that the stadium sing-along was her idea and that she pitched the performance to the team.

"That was an incoming call for them," she says. "I just said, 'I have this idea. Can I come perform with you?' And they were like, 'Sure.' That was the extent of the conversation."

As the Bananas faced off against the Indianapolis Clowns in Denver, Bell emerged from the stands and made her way down to the field dressed in a custom Bananas jersey and leopard-print cargo pants. The crowd cheered, and Bell broke out into song, starting with Frozen 's "For the First Time in Forever."

"I can't wait to meet everyone — what if I meet the one ?" the star — who famously voices the character of Anna in the Frozen films — quipped as the music played.

Bell was then joined by Klena, 34, as he sang "Dancing Through Life" from Wicked. The two danced together before going into "(I've Had) the Time of My Life" from Dirty Dancing — completing the number by performing the iconic lift from the 1987 film.

Bell tells PEOPLE that pulling off the lift was "the most surprising thing" about the performance.

"I had in my head this awesome vision of being in the Dirty Dancing lift, but we only had 30 minutes of rehearsal, and I maybe jumped into Derek Klena's arms seven times prior to that one you saw on the Internet," she reveals.

"But the whole thing was a freaking dream come true," she adds.

The Bananas shared a video of Bell and Klena's performance on Instagram at the time, writing, "The mashup we never knew we needed🤩."

Klena commented on the post, "The kindest, most talented human! @kristenanniebell you are truly the GOAT!! 🔥🔥🔥👏👏👏."

Other celebrities also shared their praise for Bell's performance, including Reese Witherspoon , who wrote, "AHHHHH!!!! Making the Bananas even more magical !! 🍌 ✨."

This Is Us star Chrissy Metz commented, "This is my kind of baseball!"

Days before her appearance at the Bananas game, Bell shared photos on her Instagram Stories on Aug. 12 showing herself arriving at the Disney Animation Studios building in Burbank, Calif., as production began on Frozen 3 , which is set for a 2027 theatrical release.

In one photo, Bell and her dog, Frank , can be seen walking into the building. In another, Frank posed for a photo in front of Frozen animation drawings of characters Anna and Elsa (voiced by Idina Menzel ).

"Accompanied by my temporary admin assistant," Bell captioned the post.

On Aug. 14, Bell, Menzel, 55, and Josh Gad (voice of Olaf) reunited at D23: The Ultimate Disney Fan Event to preview Frozen 3. In an early look at the third installment of the hit animated franchise, the trio explained that Frozen 3 will show Anna and Kristoff ( Jonathan Groff ) getting married, as well as Olaf falling in love.

Frozen 3 will be released in theaters on Nov. 24, 2027.

articles.title: Tourists return to Las Vegas despite soaring prices that drove visitors away
articles.summary: Las Vegas topped Priceline's search list for September 2026 as visitor numbers inch upward, but rising costs and a 30% drop in Canadian travelers loom large.
articles.body: Las Vegas tourism may have taken a hit last year — but new data suggests that Sin City may be showing signs of life again. Las Vegas topped Priceline's list of U.S. destinations with the biggest year-over-year increase in searches for September, beating out Orlando and New York, the New York Post reported. The city also welcomed 2.7% more visitors in July compared with the same month last year, according to the Las Vegas Convention and Visitors Authority (LVCVA). LAS VEGAS PRICES SQUEEZE EVERYDAY TRAVELERS AS POPULAR CITY EMBRACES EXPENSIVE MAKEOVER That marks a partial recovery after visitation fell 12% in July 2025. Hotel occupancy in July rose 1.1 percentage points year over year to 77.2%, while convention attendance fell 5.6%, according to the LVCVA. Vegas' signs of life come amid frustration from tourists over the rising cost of visiting the city. A $26 minibar bottle of water at Aria, for example, sparked social media outrage in 2025 after a guest's complaint was published by travel blog "View from the Wing" and picked up by The Las Vegas Review-Journal. It became a symbol of complaints that visitors were being nickel-and-dimed in Vegas. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The city has yet to fully recover to its pre-pandemic tourism levels. In 2025, Las Vegas welcomed 38.5 million visitors, down 7.5% from 2024, according to the LVCVA. Visitor spending fell to $50.8 billion that year, down from $55.1 billion in 2024, according to a report presented to the LVCVA board. LVCVA President and CEO Steve Hill told the Nevada Economic Forum earlier this month that annual visitor volume remains about 10% below the 42.5 million visitors recorded in 2019. The city has yet to fully recover to its pre-pandemic tourism levels. One major factor is the decline in Canadian travelers, historically Las Vegas' largest international market. Canadian visitation is down about 30% from 2019 levels, Hill said, while airfare to and from Las Vegas has climbed more than 20% in recent months, according to reports. "We are still gradually losing leisure travelers," Hill told the panel. "But right now our convention attendance is so strong that it is more than overcoming that number." Las Vegas visitors are also getting wealthier, and fewer of them are in their 20s. In 2025, 75% of visitors earned $100,000 or more, according to the LVCVA, and 44% earned $150,000 or more, News 3 Las Vegas reported. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Meanwhile, visitation among tourists ages 21 to 29 has fallen more than 10% since 2022, according to the LVCVA. "Gaming was once the dominant revenue driver," luxury travel expert Whytney Rawls previously told Fox News Digital. "Today, a much larger share comes from premium room rates, luxury dining, nightlife, entertainment, retail and large-scale events." Vegas has evolved to capitalize on booming luxury travel by increasingly catering to wealthy clientele, Rawls added. Lavish new restaurants, upgraded hospitality packages and high-profile events such as the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix illustrate the city's push toward premium experiences. The Sphere grossed $379 million on 1.7 million tickets sold in 2025, making it the world's highest-grossing arena for the year, according to Pollstar data reported by The Wall Street Journal. articles.title: Carrot Top Cancels Las Vegas Shows Amid Hospitalization
articles.summary: Prop comic "is recovering in the hospital and is receiving the care and support he needs," rep says in statement
articles.body:
Carrot Top was forced to cancel his Las Vegas shows this weekend after the prop comic was hospitalized on Friday night.

A rep for the red-haired comedian born Scott Thompson confirmed in a statement, "Mr. Thompson is recovering in the hospital and is receiving the care and support he needs. His family and those closest to him are deeply grateful for the concern, prayers and respectfully ask for privacy."

TMZ reported Friday that Thompson was rushed to the hospital following a suicide attempt; the comedian's rep did not elaborate on the cause of the hospitalization or Thompson's condition.

Due to the situation, Thompson canceled both his Friday and Saturday shows at Las Vegas' Luxor, where Carrot Top has held a residency for 21 years. As of press time, the comic is scheduled to perform Monday night at that venue.

Best known for his wild hair and zany onstage antics — which include diving into a bottomless chest of humorous props — Carrot Top has starred in films like his own Chairman of the Board and Pauly Shore Is Dead , and has appeared as himself on TV shows like the Vegas-set CSI , Reno 911! , and most recently Hacks .

articles.summary: Clay Aiken revealed he "died inside" after Rosie O'Donnell outed him on "The View" during a heated 2006 exchange with Kelly Ripa over a viral moment.

"I died inside a lot that week," he said. "I got woken up by my son's mother who said, 'Um, you need to wake up because Rosie just outed you on 'The View.' I woke up. I was freaked out." articles.title: Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.
articles.summary: "There's an epidemic affecting our nation's young people. The epidemic is fear." As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Fe...
articles.body:
Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Were Clowned for Buying the Staten Island Ferry. They Just Proved Everyone Wrong.

"There's an epidemic affecting our nation's young people. The epidemic is fear."

As I scrolled through Instagram on my ride downtown to the Snapple Island Ferry Comedy Show, a reel from The Free Press popped up. Professor Arthur Brooks was making the case that "Gen Z is perhaps the most risk-averse generation in history."

Now, I'm no psychologist. I'm a social media editor. And I theorize that some of that fear Brooks describes comes from our overexposure to a digital world that, seemingly, has all the answers. And when someone makes a decision outside the purview of algorithmic logic — like buying an abandoned ferry for $280,000 at a city auction — they are at the mercy of, well, being completely clowned .

That's exactly what the news cycle did to Pete Davidson and Colin Jost after they joined a group of investors to buy the decommissioned John F. Kennedy in 2022. Built in 1965, the JFK was the oldest ferry in the Staten Island fleet when it was retired last August due to mechanical failures. Davidson and Jost intended to transform the vessel into a floating entertainment venue. "Davidson, who's no longer with SNL, might need to call his agent to book those gigs — turning the 57-year-old ship into a nightspot is likely to cost millions," The New York Daily News reported . The headline read: "Retired NY Ferry Bought by Pete Davidson and Colin Jost Is Full of Asbestos, Roaches, Say Ex-Crew Members."

The social media hate laid on thick, too: "Have you heard of the hottest club in the city?" one person tweeted ( per the LA Times ). "It's called 'Tetanus' and it's located in the rusted belly of a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry. You'll dance the night away while also always being just moments away from drowning."

Years had passed without hearing about the ferry until I got an unexpected email in my inbox: "EMBARGOED: Invite to NYC's Most Unexpected Comedy Club From Pete Davidson and Colin Jost."

As it turned out, the "SNL" comedians partnered with Snapple to give New Yorkers an "unexpectedly refreshing break from the daily grind," transforming their vessel into the Snapple Staten Island Ferry for a free, one-night-only floating comedy show.

Could the comedians have listed tickets for $200 a pop and still packed the ferry? Undoubtedly. Instead, they dropped a limited batch of free tickets at 3 p.m. each day (Sept. 3-8). The resulting buzz and scramble among young New Yorkers to secure tickets (not totally unlike the IMAX 70mm frenzy surrounding "The Odyssey" ) was much more valuable than the low six figures a sold-out show might have grossed at the door. Those lucky enough to make it aboard became a test audience for two brand comebacks, each fiercely looking to win over a younger generation before betting on a much bigger, more calculated swing.

The first is Snapple, which started phasing out its signature glass bottles in 2017, replacing them with plastic (the transition was complete by 2021). The company justified the brand's "massive makeover" as a decision made "with the evolution of sustainability in mind." The operational savings from slashing the cost of manufacturing a bottle to roughly a third of what it once was probably looked pretty savory to the big-wig execs at Keurig Dr Pepper. Consumers weren't as quenched.

Snapple eventually budged in the fall of 2025, launching a limited glass-bottle revival at select bodegas and retailers across New York, citing a "demand for nostalgia from an OVERWHELMING number of consumers." The brand has yet to commit to a wider or permanent return, but it was clearly testing the waters with this major brand activation.

Hosting Snapple's revival party was Davidson and Jost's own comeback project to replenish the New York comedy scene, taking the form of a floating, popsicle-orange vessel. They once played the purchase off as a joke on "SNL," with Jost quipping, "We thought the whole thing through" (sarcasm implied). But four years later, this one-night-only comedy show offered them a real opportunity to float their idea.

The main room was packed. Because the ferry, naturally, didn't have one big corridor, an overflow room projected a live feed of the main stage (shaped like a blocky 'T').

"You're media, right?" an event coordinator asked me. "Yes!" I had zoned out. "Then we better put you up here." She whisked me straight to the front and pointed at two young women, who immediately jolted to their feet and shuffled toward the far end of the bench running parallel to the stage. "I, uh, I'm sorry I took your seats," I told the two women as I sidestepped past them. They glanced at each other and giggled. "It's okay," one of them said. "Trust me."

It took me a couple of minutes to figure out what she meant. Then I pulled out my phone to take a picture of the stage: a black barstool, a (glass!) Peach Tea Snapple and a mic stand. I wasn't just in the front row. I was in the hot seat. The very hot seat, directly under the mic stand. Stage lights beamed down on me, and the ferry cabin itself was extremely muggy. (I guess in Davidson and Jost's master plan, A/C hit the cutting room floor.)

The room skewed younger millennials and older Gen Z. Most toward the front looked like (or probably were) influencers who'll look good on camera. Usually, I'll recognize at least a few media friends in a crowd like this. Not here. I tried making friendly banter with the dude sitting next to me. He was cordial, but his energy read: Nope.

At nine o'clock sharp, the lights went dark. Davidson and Jost emerged from beneath the neon Snapple Island Ferry sign to rapturous applause. This would be the first and last time we'd see the two co-hosts all night.

I've encountered Davidson and Jost in the wild before, but this tight vantage point popped any illusion of celebrity. Picture sitting in the front row of a movie theater.

"This is something we've wanted to do for like five years, so thank you guys for coming out," Davidson opened. "And thank you to our sponsor, Snapple." After holding a beat for the applause, Davidson exclaimed, "The glass is back, baby!"

Jost added: "I also feel like we should acknowledge our former sponsor: my accountant's suicide note." He smirked. "Snapple asked me to say this."

They then turned to the first of three lingering storylines from the news cycle they clearly wanted to address. First, the aforementioned clowning. "The amount of shit that people have talked," Davidson said. "Well, suck it!"

"Everyone feeling hot and nauseous? That's a good feeling," Jost asked the crowd before moving on to news topic numero dos. "Obviously we'll get going soon. We're gonna stop at the Strait of Hormuz." But when Jost looked over at Davidson to tee up the next punchline, it became clear the geopolitical reference sailed right over his head.

"I like how you thought I would know what that is," Davidson quipped back. He glanced down at the shot clock. 8:17 remaining. The sweat was palpable.

"I love that this is our body language," Davidson said, leaning into their candid awkwardness as he and Jost stood marooned on opposite ends of the oversized T-shaped stage. "It's truly like we're waiting for someone to start a fight."

Laughing along with the crowd, Jost admitted, "We don't know exactly what to do." The audience roared. That unvarnished honesty, the willingness to take themselves down a notch, clearly resonated with the audience of young people accustomed to spending hours each day swiping through content engineered to mask imperfection.

"We have an incredible show. There are so many great comedians here," Jost said. "Macklemore is here tonight." The crowd erupted. Jost stalled on a few uhs, his eyes scanning the room as he debated whether it was worth taking the joke any further.

Davidson took advantage of the moment. "You wanted to make a stance tonight, right?" he poked. "Colin was talking mad shit backstage, dude. He was like, 'Macklemore doesn't have shit on what I'm about to say.'"

Red in the face, Jost quickly rowed back to safer waters. "So, in other news…" From there, the remainder of their opener centered on Davidson's recent concussion. But the lineup of fierce rising comics (with considerably less to lose) didn't shy away from the insecurities and taboos their Gen Z audience might be too anxious to confront.

Matt Richards, who served as emcee for the night (effectively filling the role many of us presumed Davidson and Jost would play), set the tone for the night by chugging an entire Snapple in one go and then telling a story of how he tried to suck his own penis as a teenager. "Happy to say it didn't work out," Richards said. "If it did, I wouldn't be here." In an alternate timeline, he'd "live under a bridge and suck my own dick all day."

As the crowd observed Richards, he gauged their reactions, taking the temperature of how far he could push them. The other comics were about to dive into some risqué material — he was just warming them up.

Richards wiped a bulk of sweat from his forehead. The humidity was becoming hard to ignore. Playfully, he advised Davidson and Jost to sort out the A/C situation before the next show. That's what I was thinking.

When Chris Rock sat down with Variety's Selome Hailu for his first in-depth interview since "The Slap," he recalled "dying a death" during a stand-up set in Oakland in '96. He was workshopping his controversial "Black People Versus N—s" bit, which would eventually appear in his landmark HBO special "Bring the Pain" that helped catapult Rock into rock-star comic status.

"People wanted to fight because I didn't have it right yet," Rock explained in his cover story interview . "You gotta go over the line to find the line. That's what people don't understand. When a comedian gets in trouble for saying something at the club, it's like, 'Dude, that's what the club's for.'"

Overcoming the fear of vulnerability, on both sides of the stage, is what makes the club special. A physical vessel where smartphones, despite the event's plea for ample social coverage, were repeatedly told to stay tucked away.

At one point, a Staten Island photographer named Sean lowered his camera to snap a portrait on his phone of "Impractical Jokers" star Sal Vulcano mid-set. Vulcano immediately stopped. "No cellphones, sir," he said. "It's right up in my face." Sean held up his DSLR, cutting Vulcano's budding rant short.

"This guy's just like- oh, you work here?" Vulcano said, his tone instantly changing. "Okay, you're not fired. You're great. I love you."

Even an Impractical Joker, after hundreds of public challenges and punishments designed to push the limits of embarrassment, could still tense up when a cellphone camera caught him experimenting with a new bit. "That was the ending," he told the crowd after telling a story about buying health insurance for his newborn. "I thought that would get a bigger laugh."

The crowd loved it. He was hyper-fixated on grading his performance.

Perhaps that's why crowd work is so effective. Is there any other setting better designed to experience a flash of public humiliation? "I like this guy," Richards said, pointing at me. "You look like a Disney villain."

Caitlin Peluffo stormed the stage with material in the — let's call it — advanced workshopping stages. After boldly announcing to the crowd that she was "dropping eggs," she turned to ask if I knew what ovulating was.

I responded with a sarcastic "Ehh!" and bobbed my head. "Go figure," she said. "I wouldn't expect anything less from a man wearing khakis."

After another minute or two of hyper-sexual jokes, she circled back to me.

I froze. Then hit her with the same ambiguous emote.

"You're really wishy-washy on the answer, sir."

"Those pants aren't leaving any mystery, I'll tell you that," she fired back. "You're not circumcised, I can tell." The crowd woo-ed. "That's okay. I like me a full-body boy," she continued. "I'm not an easy cum. You better crack your knuckles."

I cracked my knuckles on both hands. She smiled. Peluffo got what she needed from me. Mercifully, she moved on to her next victim.

"Are you a tough cum or an easy cum?" she asked an attractive, reserved young woman. "Which one are you?" I had never seen a face more red in my entire life. "ANSWER THE FUCKING QUESTION!"

"Fuck!" Peluffo shot back. "You're probably cumming right now."

On the way out, ferry workers dressed in sailor uniforms were handing departing guests free Snapple. I grabbed a glass peach tea and popped a squat on the pier. It really does taste better.

As I sat there taking in the night, the sound of clinking glass got louder and louder. Sure enough, I spotted a small procession bolting away from the boat with entire cases of Snapple.

I walked over and asked a few of the workers why they were giving them away. A woman with a dyed-blonde bob leaned toward me, lowering her voice.

"Please, take one now and leave before anyone sees you," she said. "We need to get rid of all of these before the end of the night."

articles.title: Converse pulls ad after claims it appeared to show a KKK lynching
articles.summary: The backlash also resurfaced a separate Converse campaign featuring sneakers hanging from a tree
articles.body:
Converse has apologized and pulled a sneaker ad after online backlash over imagery critics compared to the Ku Klux Klan and lynching.

The ad featured K-pop star Karina standing beneath a star-shaped spotlight holding a pair of black high-top Converse sneakers, with the lighting making her silhouette resemble a KKK hood and the sneakers drawing comparisons to a lynching victim.

Converse, owned by Nike, acknowledged the mistake, removed the ad from its channels, and vowed to do better, but the controversy continued as fans and public figures criticized the campaign for its racist imagery.

Converse has apologized and pulled a sneaker ad after online backlash over imagery critics compared to the Ku Klux Klan and lynching .

The ad, part of Converse's global campaign for its Chuck 70 X sneaker, featured K-pop star Karina of the group Aespa standing beneath a star-shaped spotlight while holding a pair of black high-top Converse sneakers. She wore a long white skirt, while the lighting made her silhouette look to many social media users like a KKK hood, with the dangling sneakers drawing comparisons to a lynching victim.

The Chuck 70 X was released globally on August 27, and the controversial image was posted to Converse's social media accounts earlier this month. But the backlash intensified after social media users circulated an uncropped version of the advertisement, which they said made the resemblance to a pointed hood and hanging body more apparent.

Converse, which is owned by Nike , told The Independent in a statement: "We're sorry. We understand why this image is deeply upsetting and recognize that we got this wrong. We removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened and we will do better."

Still, fans and public figures alike continued to share their thoughts on the ad.

"No, you're not crazy. Yes, the Converse ad is racist. Yes, it looks like a Klan outfit. Yes, it looks like a lynching. And no, 'it's just a shoe ad' is not a defense," one fan wrote on X.

Chicago-based photographer Stephanie Schwartz criticized the campaign on Threads, writing: "Shadow, light, and composition. Every photographer can tell you, whoever did this ad knew EXACTLY what they were doing."

Actress Yvette Nicole Brown also reacted to the campaign on Threads, writing: "That's a lynching, yes?"

The controversy also resurfaced a separate Converse campaign featuring footwear in a tree. The image, created for a collaboration with Copenhagen-based lifestyle brand Palmes, showed a person standing on a ladder with a pair of sneakers hanging from a tree branch. The image was reportedly released on September 14, Adweek reports.

Social media users shared the image alongside the Karina ad, saying the two campaigns together heightened concerns about the imagery.

One Threads user described the second image as doubling down on the symbolism, while another posted them side-by-side, writing : "There is NO REASON why WE should see an advertisement & immediately think of Strange Fruit by Billie Holiday."

articles.standfirst: Cantora intensifica presença no circuito dos festivais, como convidada de outros artistas ou como atração principal, em movimento iniciado em 2022.
articles.summary: Cantora intensifica presença no circuito dos festivais, como convidada de outros artistas ou como atração principal, em movimento iniciado em 2022.
articles.body:
Maria Bethânia é presença confirmada no line-up da edição de 2027 do Festival de Verão de Salvador — Foto: Guilherme Nabhan / Divulgação

♬ A confirmação de Maria Bethânia no line-up da 26ª edição da Festival de Verão de Salvador – em apresentação agendada para 23 de janeiro de 2027 na Arena Festival, na capital da Bahia – sinaliza que a cantora entra de vez e com força na era dos festivais, seja como convidada de algum artista ou como uma das atrações principais.

Assim que caiu o pano do show comemorativo dos 60 anos de carreira da artista, apresentado em curta turnê que foi de setembro de 2025 a janeiro deste ano de 2026, Bethânia passou a se apresentar basicamente no circuito de festivais, em movimento que vem se intensificando desde a primeira apresentação da cantora nesse modelo atual de festival, em 2022, no paulistano Coala Festival.

Bethânia segue movimento já feito pelo mano Caetano Veloso e se torna nome já recorrente em festivais. Além de ter sido convidada de Paulinho da Viola na apresentação do sambista no festival carioca Doce Maravilha, em 8 de agosto, a cantora criou um show solo próprio para festival, estreado em 22 de agosto, em Vitória da Conquista (BA), no Festival de Inverno da Bahia.

O roteiro desse show – que inclui samba ainda inédito em disco, “Luz e clarão” (Xande de Pilares e Gustavo Clarão, 2026), composto em memória da mãe da artista, Dona Canô (1907 – 2012) – foi a base da apresentação da cantora no Coala Festival no sábado retrasado, 12 de setembro. E certamente dará o norte dos próximos shows de Bethânia no festival Clássicos do Brasil – em apresentação agendada para 28 de novembro, na cidade do Rio de Janeiro (RJ) – e no Festival de Verão de Salvador 2027.

Além de interessante, por vir de intérprete consagrada pelo estilo teatral de interpretação moldada para shows feitos em espaços menores, esse movimento de Maria Bethânia em direção aos festivais é benéfico tanto para a artista quanto para as plateias desses eventos.

A cantora renova o público de forma natural, se apresentando para plateia composta por seguidores de outros artistas – um público que talvez descubra ali, em um festival, o magnetismo singular da intérprete, senhora da cena.

Enfim, Maria Bethânia está firme e forte na era dos festivais, e tudo indica que veio para ficar.

articles.title: Álbum do século XX: fotógrafa localiza família após achado no RS | G1
articles.standfirst: Fotos atravessaram décadas, passaram por um antiquário e mobilizaram desconhecidos até voltarem às mãos dos netos de Eunice e João.
articles.summary: Fotos atravessaram décadas, passaram por um antiquário e mobilizaram desconhecidos até voltarem às mãos dos netos de Eunice e João.
articles.body:
Fotografias guardam mais do que rostos. Guardam datas, lugares, afetos e fragmentos de vidas inteiras. Além disso, toda fotografia faz uma promessa silenciosa: a de impedir que um instante desapareça por completo.

Quando a fotógrafa Mayara Stuelp, 22 anos, encontrou um antigo álbum sendo vendido por R$ 20 em uma tradicional feira de artesanato, artes plásticas e antiguidades na Região Central de Porto Alegre , não imaginava que as 33 imagens em preto e branco que vinham junto da compra a levariam a uma investigação que levaria décadas.

A busca que levou duas semanas terminou com a localização dos familiares de um casal retratado nas fotografias e a devolução de um acervo capaz de resgatar lembranças que poderiam ter se perdido para sempre.

Álbum comprado pela fotógrafa Mayara Stuelp, em feira de Porto Alegre — Foto: Divulgação/ Mayara Stuelp

Em um domingo de julho, durante um passeio pelo Brique da Redenção, Mayara encontrou entre os antiquários um álbum grande , de couro e a preço acessível: custava R$ 20 .

As imagens contavam a história de uma família. Mais especificamente, de um casal: ali estavam Eunice e João .

Sem saber, Mayara acabava de embarcar em uma investigação que mobilizaria historiadores, curiosos, genealogistas amadores e milhares de pessoas nas redes sociais até resultar na devolução de um pedaço da história daquela família.

Ao seguir as pistas deixadas nas fotografias, ela reconstruiu parte da trajetória deles, um casal que viveu em Porto Alegre ao longo do século passado .

"Como aquelas fotos foram parar ali?" foi a pergunta que deu início a tudo.

Aos 22 anos, Mayara trabalha com fotografia documental . Desde sempre, diz ter fascínio por memórias, registros e histórias de vida.

Quando folheou rapidamente o álbum antes da compra, percebeu que havia algo diferente. As fotografias eram bonitas. Bem conservadas. Mostravam momentos espontâneos, sem poses rígidas . Havia uma familiaridade estética entre aquelas imagens e o trabalho que ela produz.

"Eu me identificava com aquelas fotografias. Parecia que as pessoas não estavam posando. Era algo muito próximo do que eu gosto de fazer", conta.

O plano inicial era restaurar o álbum e utilizá-lo para guardar suas próprias fotografias impressas. Mas as imagens que encontrou dentro dele começaram a provocar perguntas.

Atrás de algumas fotos havia nomes, datas, endereços e dedicatórias. Eram pistas aparentemente pequenas, mas suficientes para despertar a curiosidade de Mayara. Foi a partir desses fragmentos de informação que ela começou a reconstruir a trajetória do casal, pesquisando registros antigos e buscando familiares.

"Eu ficava lembrando que as fotos estavam ali e ia pesquisar de novo. Aos poucos fui ficando obcecada pela história", revela.

No entanto, o que mais a intrigava não era descobrir quem eram Eunice e João. Era entender como toda aquela memória havia terminado à venda entre objetos usados .

"Em todos os antiquários de Porto Alegre a gente vê centenas de fotografias e álbuns sendo vendidos. Mas ninguém sabe exatamente o que aconteceu para aquelas memórias irem parar lá", comenta.

Com poucas pistas em mãos, Mayara e o namorado iniciaram uma espécie de quebra-cabeça genealógico.

Percebendo o potencial da história, a fotógrafa decidiu publicar um vídeo nas redes sociais. Foi quando centenas de mensagens começaram a chegar. Algumas pessoas apenas queriam saber o final daquela história, outras resolveram participar da busca.

Houve quem pesquisasse arquivos históricos, documentos antigos e acervos de jornais. E uma ajuda decisiva veio de Curitiba: durante noites seguidas, uma pesquisadora quis ajudar e mergulhou em acervos e documentos históricos, enviando informações que ajudaram a conectar as peças daquele quebra-cabeça.

"O vídeo virou uma pesquisa coletiva", resume Mayara.

Álbum comprado pela fotógrafa Mayara Stuelp, em feira de Porto Alegre, tinha fotos de Eunice e João — Foto: Divulgação/ Mayara Stuelp

O álbum carregava registros de diferentes fases da vida do casal. Fotos de eventos sociais, viagens, retratos familiares e cenas do cotidiano.

Inclusive, uma imagem de infância revelou uma informação crucial: Eunice havia nascido em 1922 . Outra mostrava que ela tocava piano.

A busca pela identidade de quem estava nas fotos revelou que Eunice tinha uma forte ligação com o Instituto de Educação de Porto Alegre. Aos 17 anos, estudava na instituição .

Anos depois, tornou-se professora de piano e canto no mesmo local . Também ajudou a fundar uma associação de ex-alunas do Instituto de Educação.

Enquanto isso, a história de João também começava a emergir: a certidão de casamento do casal , datada de 24 de setembro de 1946, revelou que o nome original de João Batista era Giambattista .

No álbum, também havia duas fotografias com dedicatórias escritas em italiano . Segundo a investigação feita por Mayara, João chegou ainda criança ao Brasil e, ao longo da vida, passou a utilizar a versão brasileira do nome .

Mesmo com tantas informações, faltava o principal: alguém da família estaria vivo?

Durante as buscas, surgiram nomes de netas do casal. Em agosto, Mayara encontrou um perfil nas redes sociais.

"Fiquei na dúvida se eu deveria ou não mandar mensagem porque poderia ser estranho. Eu não tinha certeza se era de fato elas", relembra.

Depois de enviar uma mensagem para uma das netas, a fotógrafa não recebeu resposta e chegou a acreditar que a busca terminaria ali. Dias depois, após a repercussão do vídeo publicado na internet, a neta reconheceu os avós nas fotografias e respondeu Mayara.

As duas passaram a conversar por mensagens. A neta enviou fotografias dos avós já idosos e contou detalhes da família.

Foi quando veio a resposta do porquê o álbum estaria no Centro de Porto Alegre: Mayara conta que Eunice morreu há cerca de dois anos e, provavelmente, o álbum se perdeu quando o apartamento foi vendido .

Na última semana, Mayara enviou as fotografias pelos Correios para Santa Catarina, onde a neta mora. Junto delas, foi toda a documentação reunida durante a investigação: certidões, registros e peças da história que a própria família desconhecia.

Poucos dias depois, recebeu a confirmação de que o material havia chegado.

"A parte mais legal nisso tudo foi perceber uma coisa muito bonita: como histórias podem aproximar as pessoas", resume Mayara.

Agora vazio, o álbum original ficou com a fotógrafa. Ele será restaurado e ganhará uma nova história com fotografias da própria Mayara.

articles.title: Fiuk comprova que é bom de marketing ao anunciar o retorno da banda Hori em (esvaziado) show solo de 'despedida' | G1
articles.body:
Fiuk revela que continua na música, mas agora novamente como vocalista da banda Hori — Foto: Reprodução / Instagram Fiuk

♬ Pode-se questionar a relevância da carreira musical de Fiuk , mas é cada vez mais evidente o talento do cantor para gerar notícia ou factoide.

O anúncio da volta da banda Hori – feito pelo artista no palco, na noite de sexta-feira, 18 de setembro, ao fim do que deveria ter sido o show de “despedida” da carreira solo de Fiuk em Campinas (SP) – é mais uma ação de marketing que garantiu ao filho de Fábio Jr. diversas manchetes ao longo das últimas 24 horas.

Afinal, o anúncio do retorno da Hori, banda da qual Fiuk fez parte entre 2004 e 2011, foi feito somente nove dias após o cantor ter dito nas redes sociais que iria interromper a carreira musical por tempo indeterminado para seguir um “caminho diferente” após o derradeiro show, agendado para anteontem, 18 de setembro, em Campinas (SP). Revelação que já tinha gerado muita mídia para o artista.

O suposto último show solo do cantor teve um público de apenas 67 pessoas – indício de que paralisar a carreira musical poderia ser uma decisão sensata... Mas, ao que tudo indica, era mesmo jogada de marketing. Mais uma. Eis que Fiuk revelou no palco que, sim, vai continuar em cena, mas a partir de agora novamente ao lado da banda Hori.

“Por que que é o final da minha carreira de cantor? Porque a banda Hori tá de volta! Esse é o meu lugar, eu demorei muito pra entender aqui até que eu me sinto em casa. Então agora eu sou vocalista da banda Hori!”, justificou Fiuk.

Enfim, prestes a completar 36 anos em 25 de outubro, Filipe Kartalian Ayres Galvão parece querer encontrar um rumo para a carreira e para a própria vida. Ressuscitar a banda da adolescência pode simbolizar uma fuga da realidade da vida adulta. Mas não dá para negar que o objetivo foi atingido: chamar a atenção da mídia. Fiuk é bom de marketing!

articles.title: Lívia Christina é anunciada como nova cunhã-poranga do Boi Garantido | G1
articles.standfirst: Artista parintinense que ganhou projeção nacional no reality assume o cargo no lugar de Isabelle Nogueira, que deixou o posto este ano. Para a vaga de Rainha do Folclore, o boi escolheu a jovem Isabelle Alcântara.
articles.summary: A ex-Casa de Vidro do BBB 26 Lívia Christina assume o posto de Isabelle Nogueira no Boi Garantido, que também anunciou Isabelle Alcântara como Rainha do Folclore.
articles.body:
Lívia Christina performando no Festival de Parintins. — Foto: Mauro Neto/Secom

O Boi-Bumbá Garantido anunciou, na noite deste sábado (19), Lívia Christina como a nova cunhã-poranga da agremiação para o Festival Folclórico de Parintins de 2027. A parintinense, que ficou conhecida nacionalmente após participar da Casa de Vidro do BBB 26, assume o Item 9 no lugar de Isabelle Nogueira, que deixou o posto este ano. Para a vaga de rainha do folclore, ocupada por Lívia até o festival de 2026, o boi escolheu a jovem Isabelle Alcântara.

As mudanças no quadro de itens femininos foram anunciadas nas redes sociais do Garantido. Segundo a agremiação, a escolha de Lívia e Isabelle foi recebida pela torcida como uma valorização de artistas formadas dentro do próprio boi.

Lívia ganhou projeção nacional ao participar da Casa de Vidro do BBB 26. A dinâmica reuniu participantes que disputavam uma vaga no reality show da Globo. No festival, terá como adversária a também ex-BBB e cunhã-poranga do Boi Caprichoso, Marciele Albuquerque.

Lívia é natural de Parintins e começou a trajetória no grupo de dança Garantido Show. Antes de chegar ao posto de Rainha do Folclore, também defendeu o boi como porta-estandarte, função que assumiu em dezembro de 2022.

A nova função representa a mulher indígena e guerreira da Amazônia nas apresentações do bumbá no Bumbódromo.

A mudança também marca a sucessão de Isabelle Nogueira, que se aposentou do posto de cunhã-poranga do boi vermelho e branco depois de 9 anos. Ao longo da trajetória no Garantido, Isabelle também defendeu o posto de Rainha do Folclore entre 2015 e 2017.

Nas redes sociais, Lívia comemorou a escolha e agradeceu ao Boi Garantido, à torcida e ao novo presidente da agremiação, Marialvo Brandão.

"Meu coração transborda de emoção, meu povo!", escreveu. Ela afirmou ainda que sente "gratidão, felicidade, responsabilidade e um amor que não cabe no peito".

Lívia Christina é a nova cunhã-poranga do Boi Garantido. — Foto: Divulgação/Boi Garantido

Isabelle Alcântara é a nova Rainha do Folclore

Para ocupar o posto deixado por Lívia, o Garantido anunciou Isabelle Alcântara como nova rainha do folclore para a temporada de 2027.

Também parintinense, Isabelle integrou o Garantido Show e tem trajetória ligada à dança. É acadêmica de enfermagem e também foi cunhã-poranga do Boi Tira Prosa, que disputa o Festival Folclórico do distrito de Nova Maracanã, em Faro, no Pará.

Segundo o Garantido, Isabelle começou sua trajetória na dança ainda na infância e leva para o Bumbódromo a experiência construída dentro da cultura popular.

"Nascida e criada na Baixa do Xanda, a cunhatã que sempre respirou o Festival de Parintins traz para a arena a graça, a beleza e a ancestralidade do nosso povo", afirmou o boi em publicação nas redes sociais.

A agremiação também destacou que a trajetória da nova rainha do folclore representa o talento de artistas formadas dentro do próprio Garantido.

Isabelle Alcantara é anunciada como nova rainha do folclore do Boi Garantido. — Foto: Divulgação/Boi Garantido

articles.title: Ed Sheeran Addresses Macklemore Controversy While on Stage at First Concert Since Rapper Dropped From Tour: ‘What Is Happening in Gaza Is Catastrophic and Unjustifiable’
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore’s removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia’s Lincoln...
articles.body:
Ed Sheeran addressed the controversy surrounding Macklemore's removal from his Loop Tour on Saturday night, speaking from the stage at Philadelphia's Lincoln Financial Field during his first concert since the rapper was dropped from the trek.

"Before I play some songs tonight, I hope it's okay if I say a few words about this last week," Sheeran said at the top of Saturday's show. "I'm used to my music being criticized, and I'm always happy to take that because I'm lucky. A lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I'm surprised. I'm not surprised that I've even done it. You know, it's normal. But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so so sorry."

Saturday's concert marked Sheeran's first performance since a tumultuous week for the U.S. leg of his Loop Tour, which saw Macklemore removed from the remaining dates following the rapper's onstage remarks in support of Palestinians during Sheeran's Sept. 4 and 5 shows at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

Sheeran continued: "I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I'm here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour."

During his MetLife performances, Macklemore spoke about the war in Gaza and the West Bank and told the stadium crowd "free Palestine." His set also included "Hind's Hall," his 2024 protest song supporting Palestinians. The remarks drew criticism from some Jewish and pro-Israel organizations, including the Israeli-American Council, which called for Macklemore to be removed from the tour.

Messina Touring Group, the promoter behind the U.S. leg of the Loop Tour, subsequently announced that Macklemore would no longer appear on the remaining dates. The company said venues had informed the promoter that they would not allow concerts featuring Macklemore to proceed, a situation it said could have resulted in cancellations affecting hundreds of thousands of ticket holders.

While Sheeran addressed the decision in a statement earlier this week , stressing that Macklemore's removal was made by the promoter and venues rather than by him, he again acknowledged that he is "deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performance." "This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world," he said.

Sheeran also said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," describing the suffering caused by the war as a "human tragedy," while explaining that he has generally sought to keep his concerts focused on "unity, joy, escapism, love" rather than his own political views.

Macklemore responded to his removal in a lengthy statement of his own, saying that he and Sheeran had held "difficult conversations" in the aftermath of the MetLife shows. While expressing respect for Sheeran personally, the rapper challenged the singer's preference for remaining publicly neutral and said he did not regret using the tour stage to speak in support of Palestinians. Macklemore has since said he will donate $1 million to Palestinian relief organizations.

The fallout quickly spread beyond Macklemore. Singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe and Danish band Lukas Graham, who had been expected to support Sheeran on upcoming North American dates, both withdrew from the tour. Finneas, who was scheduled to join Sheeran for a run of South American dates later this year, also pulled out, while Irish folk group Beoga — longtime collaborators who had been performing as part of Sheeran's live show — exited as well. All four cited Macklemore's removal in announcing their decisions.

The Philadelphia date nevertheless proceeded as scheduled Saturday at Lincoln Financial Field, kicking off the next stretch of Sheeran's U.S. stadium run.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran Breaks Silence on Israel-Gaza at First Show Amid Tour Controversy: ‘I Cannot Hide How I Feel About It Anymore’
articles.summary: “This has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet," Sheeran s...
articles.body:
Ed Sheeran took the stage on Saturday night for the first time since Macklemore was removed from his stadium tour following the Seattle rapper's onstage speech in support of Palestinians. The singer, who did not have any opening acts at the Philadelphia show, addressed the backlash at the top of his set.

"This is not usually how I would open the show, but before I play some songs tonight, I hope it's okay if I say a few words about this last week," he said, visibly shaken as he spoke. "I'm used to my music being criticized, and I'm always happy to take that because I'm lucky a lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest, I'm surprised. I'm not surprised that other people don't. It's normal. But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so so sorry."

He continued: "I don't want to disappoint fans, and I've never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. My concerts have always been a safe space for everyone, and that matters hugely to me. Honoring my commitment to my fans is also completely essential to who I am, and that is why I'm here tonight on my own and continuing my current tour."

In a statement earlier this week , Sheeran said the decision to nix Macklemore from the tour wasn't his, instead pointing the finger at promoter Messina Touring Group and citing pressure from venues. He said that after hearing some venues did not want Macklemore to perform following his comments at MetLife Stadium, he spoke with the owners, including Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who ultimately forced his hand.

"I am deeply worried about the idea that venues should pre-approve content for performers," Sheeran said Saturday. "This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world."

Sheeran then directly addressed his stance on the Israel-Gaza conflict, reiterating that he has never wanted to be an "activist musician" or "political commentator" but that after fans began making assumptions about where he aligns politically, he felt it was important to set the record straight himself.

"Now, I want to address the question of where I stand on Israel and Palestine, and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand," he said. "I have tried in my career not to be a political commentator of any kind, because I want my music and shows to be about unity, not division; about humanity, not politics. But this is a humanitarian issue, and I cannot hide how I feel about it anymore.

"What happened in Israel and at the Nova Music Festival on October 7 was horrific and compounded centuries of Jewish pain. What is happening in Gaza is catastrophic, unjustifiable, and disproportionate. My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians' lives, of children's lives. The systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked. I am already speaking to people across the spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps victims of these terrible times, and listening and learning because I do not know enough."

Sheeran became emotional as he thanked his fans for standing by him. "I honestly am so grateful that you're here tonight with me. This concert is still a place where everyone is welcome, and everyone here can stand beside people that have opposing views, and everyone here can stand above people that they don't agree with on everything, but they could all agree on singing these songs. And these songs are about love, hope, and unity."

Following Macklemore's exit, all of Sheeran's opening acts withdrew from his Loop Tour , including Finneas, Lukas Graham, and Aaron Row. "Money doesn't give you the right to own the conversation. Nobody's bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we're allowed to acknowledge," Graham said in a statement. "This is a difficult decision, but it's one I need to stand by."

Prior to his performance of his 2017 hit "Galway Girl," Sheeran addressed the exodus, noting that he was figuring out "how am I going to get musicians to stand onstage with me in a week where no one wants to stand on stage with me?" He introduced collaborator Alicia Enstrom, who toured with Sheeran last year, alongside other musicians. "They said yes to being on stage with the knowledge that the world thought I was a certain type of person," Sheeran said. "They said yes with the knowledge that the world may hate them too for standing onstage with me."

Sheeran also admitted he removed a secondary stage out of fear for his physical safety. "I didn't know what this audience would be like tonight," he said. "I didn't know if I would have things thrown at me. I didn't know if people would be angry at me. So Philly, I apologize that today is not the usual loop show. I took the B stage out because I was afraid of what might happen if I stood in the middle."

Doubling down on his stance after his removal from the tour, Macklemore pledged to donate $1 million to Palestinian support groups and challenged Kraft "to match" him. Kraft responded with a statement and said that "Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis." A rep for Sheeran did not immediately respond to Rolling Stone 's earlier request for comment.

articles.title: 'VIBE' box office collection day 2: Kunal Khemu and Preity Zinta's film records 55.9% growth; earns Rs 2.65 cr on Saturday
articles.summary: Kunal Khemu's 'VIBE' recorded an increase in its box office earnings on Saturday, September 19. The action thriller comedy earned Rs 2.65 cr in India .
articles.body: Kunal Khemu's 'VIBE' recorded an increase in its box office earnings on Saturday, September 19. The action thriller comedy earned Rs 2.65 cr in India net on Day 2, according to Sacnilk. The movie was screened across 2,979 shows on its first Saturday. The latest collection marks a 55.9% rise over the Rs 1.70 cr earned on its opening day. 'VIBE' registered 14% overall occupancy across 3,194 shows on Friday. Its occupancy increased to 21% on Saturday.'VIBE' earns Rs 2.65 cr on Day 2The second-day earnings have taken 'VIBE' to a total India net collection of Rs 4.35 cr. Its India gross collection currently stands at Rs 5.22 cr. The movie recorded Rs 1.70 cr on Day 1 before adding Rs 2.65 cr on Saturday. Its show count stood at 3,194 on Friday and 2,979 on Saturday.The increase in collections came alongside a rise in audience occupancy. The film's overall occupancy moved from 14% on its opening day to 21% on Day 2.Saturday occupancy reaches 21.92%The Hindi 2D version of 'VIBE' recorded 21.92% overall occupancy on Saturday. Morning shows registered 9.23% occupancy. Afternoon screenings recorded 22.15%. Evening shows registered 23.62%. Night screenings recorded the highest occupancy at 32.69%.The movie had 3,194 shows on Day 1, with overall occupancy at 14%. On Day 2, the show count was 2,979 and occupancy reached 21%.Kunal Khemu returns as writer-directorKunal Khemu has written, produced and directed 'VIBE'. He also stars in the movie alongside Preity Zinta, Sparsh Shrivastava and Vanshika Dhir. The film marks Kunal Khemu's second directorial venture after 'Madgaon Express', which was released in 2024. It also marks his debut as a producer.The project comes after more than three decades of Kunal Khemu's acting career. He previously took on writing and directing duties with 'Madgaon Express'. Vanshika Dhir makes her acting debut with 'VIBE'. She appears alongside Kunal Khemu, Preity Zinta and Sparsh Shrivastava.'VIBE' follows two friendsThe story of 'VIBE' revolves around two inseparable friends. Their otherwise ordinary lives take an unexpected turn and lead them into a fast-paced adventure. The two characters are forced to rely on their survival instincts as their situation becomes increasingly unpredictable. Their friendship is also tested as they face the challenges that come with their unusual journey. The movie combines action, comedy and thriller elements.ETimes rates 'VIBE' 3.5 starsETimes gave 'VIBE' 3.5 stars out of 5. The review reads, "Vibe is one of those films where the screenplay and sheer entertainment quotient elevate a fairly basic premise. The banter and comic set pieces are top-notch in the first half. The tonality shifts after the interval as the action takes over.The narrative becomes more convoluted and loses momentum in places as it packs in the terrorist plot, spy antics and increasingly outlandish twists. There are familiar tropes, too, including the Sipahi 1 pill that transforms Hardik into a fierce soldier and a surprise entry that saves the day during the climactic fight. Yet, despite these contrivances, the movie remains breezy and engaging enough to keep you invested. Hardik and Bugs’s training to become spies, in particular, makes for a hilarious track."DISCLAIMER: The box office numbers and the data in this article are compiled from public and industry sources. articles.body: Here is the full text of singer Ed Sheeran's speech before his Philadelphia concert Saturday night on the ongoing controversy after Macklemore was dropped as an opening act for making "free Palestine" comments and his other opening acts pulled out of his tour. "This is not usually how I open a show, but before I play some songs tonight I hope it’s OK if I say a few words about this last week. I’m used to my music being criticized, and I’m always happy to take that because I’m lucky a lot of you like my stuff, and to be honest I’m surprised, I’m not surprised." "But this week the criticism was about something much more important. And I’ve had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I’m so sorry. I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet. "Now, I want to address the question of where I stand in the situation in Israel and Palestine and whether my doing this concert here tonight implies where I stand. articles.body: Nicki Minaj has offered a personal explanation for her continued support of Donald Trump, saying she feels a connection with the U.S. president that goes beyond his political position. During a September 18 appearance on Fox News' 'The Ingraham Angle', the rapper spoke about her relationship with Trump and addressed criticism surrounding her decision to work with his administration.The conversation came as Minaj prepared to take part in the U.S. Small Business Administration's Million Dollar Pitch Competition, where she joined the judging panel for the September 18 event in Washington, D.C.Nicki Minaj explains her connection with Donald TrumpSpeaking with host Laura Ingraham, Minaj described Trump as someone whose personality has made an impression on her. She said, “He has inspired many people, not just me. And he's — he's fun.”Minaj went on to explain why she feels she can relate to him despite his position as president. She said, “He's not just smart, and you know, he's not just the president. But he's also someone that I can relate to, someone that, you know, every time I see him, or every time I see him speaking to other people, he's just himself.”She also described what she sees as Trump's ability to make people feel understood.“He's very — he's very grounded. It's easy to connect with him. It's easy to feel like he heard you, he understands you,” Minaj said.When discussing her personal feelings toward Trump, Minaj was equally direct. She said, “And I just — I just love him. And I'm not going to ever make excuses for that.”What Nicki Minaj said about the criticism?Minaj was also asked what she would say to people who have criticized her for working with Trump.Her response was brief. “Absolutely nothing,” she said.When Ingraham followed up, Minaj added, “I don't know why I should.”Her remarks came at a time when her association with the Trump administration has become more visible through her participation in the SBA's business competition.Nicki Minaj joins the Million Dollar Pitch CompetitionThe U.S. Small Business Administration announced on August 31 that Minaj would serve as a judge for the Million Dollar Pitch Competition. She joined entrepreneur Grant Cardone and Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia on the judging panel, with actor Dean Cain serving as host.According to the SBA's official announcement, the competition featured five finalists selected from 1,182 businesses representing all 50 states. The finalists competed for a combined $1 million in growth capital.The event was part of the SBA's Freedom 250 initiative, which highlights entrepreneurship and small businesses as the United States marks its 250th anniversary.Nicki Minaj takes on a new role outside musicThe Million Dollar Pitch Competition gives Minaj a chance to step into a different professional space. Known primarily for her music, she is also involved in business ventures, and the SBA has brought that experience into the competition through her role as a judge.During her Fox News conversation, Minaj also spoke about returning to the stage. She said she wants her shows to remain about music and entertainment rather than turning into political gatherings.Over the years, Minaj has explored opportunities beyond recording and performing. Her latest work with the SBA adds another experience to that list, allowing her to interact with entrepreneurs as they pitch their businesses and compete for financial support.Get the latest Bollywood & Entertainment News, and more. articles.body: Vijay Sethupathi clarified his recent leadership comments on Bigg Boss Tamil 10 after his remarks about leadership and responsibility sparked discussion on social media.
